The early precursor to actual concrete was a simpler mortar. A simple lime mortar can be made by heating limestone until it undergoes a chemical reaction causing it to give off carbon dioxide, which results in a highly reactive substance known as quicklime or calcium oxide. Mixing this paste with water then produces a white paste referred to as hydrated lime or slaked lime which the Romans would store in large clay jars until it was needed. Prior to use, the paste would be mixed with clean river sand and used to bind bricks or rocks, or to plaster the surface of walls. This simple lime-based mortar has been recorded to have been used as early as 2,500 B.C. in India, though the Greeks are credited with using the first highly durable concrete mix around 1,700 B.C.

It is noted in the novel that blood was added to the mortar of Citadel La Ferriere to strengthen the walls: "Every day in the middle of the parade square several bulls had their throats cut so that their blood could be added to the mortar to make the fortress impregnable." (page 114)

The process of adding blood to concrete or mortar mix has been in use almost as long as the use of concrete itself, though at the time it is unlikely the the scientific reason for this added strength was known. Now, we are aware that the reason for the added strength is that over time, blood that is mixed with the concrete, or mortar, decomposes leaving behind small bubbles and air pockets which have the effect of making the mix more durable. There is even a U.S. Patent filed for the use of blood, or "air entraining colloids" in mortar mixtures.

..The massive stone structure was built by up to 20,000 workers between 1805 and 1820 as part of a system of fortifications designed to keep the newly independent nation of Haiti safe from French incursions...The Haitians outfitted the fortress with 365 cannons of varying size.
